paragraphs: President Donald Trump said Monday that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky should get "somebody else" to negotiate a peace deal with Russia, according to the Washington Examiner. He spoke to reporters as he left the White House for a campaign rally in Kansas. The remark answered a question about Zelensky saying Trump is on the "wrong side of history" over Washington's approach to peace talks.

"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said, adding that Zelensky should have settled the war long ago. "I think that it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine," he said. He also said: "I want to see people not die."

Trump defended his diesel deal with Russia and his easing of sanctions on Moscow. The Examiner reports that some Republicans have criticized him, saying he is siding with Vladimir Putin over Zelensky. "I'm trying to get a hostage," Trump said. He said Putin is "laying off Iran" and that he is negotiating with Putin on Ukraine.

The Guardian reported that Zelensky, on a bipartisan call with Republican Sen. Thom Tillis and Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal, said Ukraine's Starlink access remains degraded. He also said disruptions to US intelligence sharing persist, including early warning of Russian ballistic missile launches. The senators said he repeated a willingness to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities as Trump has proposed, but only if Putin agrees to the same.

Asked whether he would discuss Ukraine with Putin without Zelensky present, Trump said he would do "anything … to end the war, whether somebody's there or not." Zelensky's response to the "somebody else" suggestion was not reported in the supplied articles.

President Donald Trump's approval rating has fallen to 31 percent, a record low in his political career, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll reported by Al Jazeera. The same poll found Democrats leading Republicans by 12 points when respondents were asked whether they would vote for a generic, unnamed Democrat or Republican.

Al Jazeera said disapproval of Trump has grown steadily in recent months, especially since the February 28 launch of the US-Israel war on Iran. It said the war has driven up petrol and diesel prices and had knock-on effects across the economy.

Other polls point the same way. A Washington Post/ABC/Ipsos poll, also released Monday, found a record-low approval rating of 33 percent, with 7 out of 10 respondents saying gasoline was becoming unaffordable. An NBC poll released Sunday found 71 percent of Americans said the country was on the "wrong track" and 55 percent would vote for the Democratic Party if an election were held that day.

The Guardian reported further findings from the Post and ABC polling: 66 percent of Americans believe Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself. It said 34 percent of Republicans share that view, a 12-point jump from last September.

The polls arrive as the midterm elections on November 3 approach and could determine control of the House and Senate. The Guardian reported that Trump is starting a seven-state campaign swing this week through parts of the country he carried in 2024, where it said unexpectedly tight races have raised concern among Republicans about Democratic gains.

Vice President JD Vance campaigned in Hendersonville, North Carolina, on Monday for Republican Senate nominee Michael Whatley and announced $858 million in additional Department of Transportation disaster relief funding, according to the Washington Examiner. The money is for areas still rebuilding after Hurricane Helene in 2024.

Vance said the funds will help rebuild eight major corridors destroyed by the storm, including I-40 and the Pigeon River Gorge. He credited President Trump, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Whatley's advocacy. He also said the Federal Emergency Management Agency has committed $7.5 billion to Helene recovery, and he contrasted Republicans with Democrats, saying Democrats "were doing nothing for Western North Carolina" when in power.

The Examiner reports that Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chair, trails former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee, by 9.6 points in the RealClearPolitics polling average. It says the administration has made multiple North Carolina appearances in recent weeks to help him. Trump is scheduled to rally in Greenville, North Carolina, on Tuesday.

Whatley criticized Cooper's conduct during the storm, saying he was in New York City for a climate gala when Helene hit on Sept. 27, 2024. The Examiner noted that this was incorrect. Citing NPR affiliate WFAE, it said Cooper attended a New York Times climate event on Sept. 25, 2024, and returned to North Carolina the same day. Cooper's campaign response was not included in the supplied article.
Whatley said Helene damaged or destroyed 73,000 homes, wiped out 45,000 small businesses and killed 107 people.

President Donald Trump has again urged New Mexico to change its name, writing on Truth Social that the state "should immediately change its name to New America." According to Fox News, he added: "We are not Mexico, we are the United States of America!"

Trump wrote that the new name "would add great value and prestige to the State" and that "Home Values and Incomes would rise." He also suggested the change might make what he called "Crooked Elections" in New Mexico "honest again." Fox News noted that the post offered no evidence for the election allegation and did not explain how a new name would raise property values or incomes.

Fox reports that Trump floated the idea last month by sharing a map with "Mexico" crossed out and replaced with "America," which the White House amplified on X. He also raised it on Sept. 9 at the RNC Midterm Convention, saying, "the people love the idea."

New Mexico's Democratic governor, Michelle Lujan Grisham, said at that time the name "isn't up for debate" and has been the state's "since before the United States existed." She accused the White House of focusing on a distraction while her administration worked on child care, education, health care and housing.

Fox noted that Trump's latest post lays out no formal process for a change. The state constitution says in Article I: "The name of this state is New Mexico." Fox said the proposal follows Trump's moves to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America" for federal use and the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America."

The Supreme Court said Monday that it will hear a case over admissions to magnet middle schools in Montgomery County, Maryland, according to the Washington Examiner. In Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education, the justices limited review to whether a challenger to a facially neutral admissions policy must show that the targeted racial group suffered an aggregate disparate impact relative to its share of the applicant pool.

The group, represented by the Pacific Legal Foundation, says the policy, changed in 2020, unlawfully discriminates. The new system uses "peer grouping and local norming": top students at each school, ranked by test scores, enter a lottery. The group argues this keeps out high scorers who would qualify if scores were compared countywide, and says Asian American enrollment fell.

The school board calls it a "race-neutral, race-blind lottery" and says the group did not plead facts showing disparate impact. Lower courts dismissed the suit, with the board pointing to Asian American students' acceptance rates relative to their share of the system. The Fourth Circuit said a clear statistical threshold must be met. PLF attorney Chris Kieser said a district should not defeat a claim by showing its policy did not harm enough children.

The court also took up a challenge to a nearly 160-year-old federal ban on home distilling. Arguments in both cases are expected between February and April 2027, with decisions by the end of June 2027.

Separately, the court could not act on a copyright petition, BMG Rights Management v. Vetter, because Justices Sotomayor, Gorsuch, Barrett and Jackson recused, leaving no quorum. The Fifth Circuit ruling stands. The next orders list is expected Nov. 9.

President Donald Trump said Monday that Paris will become a "Muslim city" very soon if France does not close its borders to immigrants, according to the Washington Examiner. Speaking outside the White House, he said he had long warned President Emmanuel Macron: "You're making a big mistake." He said the unrest in France is about immigration, "not schools, not anything." Vice President JD Vance also blamed immigration from developing nations in a social media post.

The French government and the reporting in Foreign Policy describe a different cause. Foreign Policy said young people are demanding education reform and denouncing high fuel costs and poor public services. The Examiner said protests began in late September over school conditions and widened over living costs and energy prices. Foreign Policy noted there is no reported evidence that undocumented migrants worsened the protests.

France announced a partial ban on protests in Paris and curfews in some areas on Monday. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said his "determination to restore order is absolute." He and the ruling coalition blamed the hard-left France Unbowed party for fomenting unrest. The far-right National Rally also blamed France Unbowed and said the riots show Macron has lost control. France Unbowed leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon supported the peaceful elements of the movement and criticized alleged police brutality.

The Interior Ministry said about 1,000 security personnel were injured, around 2,400 protesters were arrested and at least 3,000 businesses were pillaged. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez offered to resign, but Macron did not accept it. A second round of large demonstrations is scheduled for Saturday.

French authorities are facing questions over how they misjudged nationwide protests that turned into riots and looting, according to Fox News. The Interior Ministry said about 550,000 people joined 110 marches on Saturday, far above an intelligence estimate of roughly 200,000. Organizers put turnout at 800,000.

Fox reported that more than 1,500 stores were reportedly ransacked or destroyed, and rioters in Limoges burned a 19th-century city hall. Nearly 1,000 law enforcement officers and firefighters were injured, at least 2,400 people were arrested, and authorities estimate about 3,000 businesses were damaged. The Louvre remained closed Monday as student protesters blocked its entrances.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said, "in certain large cities, we lost control," and acknowledged a "lack of anticipation." He offered to resign, but President Emmanuel Macron refused and ordered a review of what the Élysée called failures in planning and intelligence. Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said, "We unquestionably failed."

Fox said the unrest began in September with school protests over teacher shortages and deteriorating buildings, then spread over living costs and public services. At an Oct. 1 crisis meeting, intelligence officials said the movement had reached a "tipping point" toward urban violence, Reuters reported.

The political fight is broadening. President Donald Trump blamed migration policies, while Fox said French authorities have not blamed immigrants and instead accuse ultra-left militants and criminals. Marine Le Pen's National Rally says Macron has lost control. The bond market's reaction, mentioned in the card summary, was not covered in the supplied text.

Egypt's parliament has postponed a vote on authorizing its armed forces to support Saudi Arabia against attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis, Al Jazeera reports. The House of Representatives said Monday the vote is adjourned to October 26.

The measure would authorize President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to approve any Saudi request for defense assistance. Saudi Arabia asked for support after the Houthis attacked Riyadh's international airport and the state oil company Saudi Aramco last week. Saudi authorities say 13 people were killed in the October 10 airport attack. El-Sisi said Egypt would take "any measure" needed to protect its Gulf allies, adding, "We're talking only about defence."

The opposition Egyptian Social Democratic Party, which holds nearly a dozen seats, told its lawmakers to abstain. It said parliament had not been given enough information on the mission's objectives, duration, cost or risks to Egyptian troops. Two of its MPs told AFP that most of its lawmakers nonetheless support the measure.
Under Egypt's constitution, sending troops on a combat mission abroad needs National Defence Council approval, which was given Sunday, and a two-thirds parliamentary majority.

Al Jazeera noted economic stakes. Saudi Arabia is due to deposit $5.3bn into Egypt's central bank this month, and many Egyptians working in Saudi Arabia send money home. Egypt's foreign minister says the Suez Canal has lost about $11bn since the Houthis began attacks in the Bab al-Mandeb strait in 2023. Turkiye and Pakistan have made their own pledges to Riyadh under a defense pact signed in August.

CoreWeave's bonds slipped into distressed territory last week, according to The Verge, by a common definition: investors demanding 1,000 basis points more in yield than they would get from government bonds. The outlet reports the company's shares are down more than 20 percent since Tuesday's close. Investor Chamath Palihapitiya noticed the distressed debt and asked whether the AI buildout was a private credit bubble.

The Verge adds that cofounder Brannin McBee told the Financial Times the company wants its debt to be investment-grade so it can borrow from insurers, whose capital he called "unlimited." CoreWeave secured its first investment-grade chip loan earlier this year. The Verge says such talk can make investors fear even more borrowing. Bloomberg quoted John Yovanovic of MetLife Investment Management as saying the problem is not that credit profiles have changed in the past year, but that "we've got another year and a half of supply coming."

As of its second-quarter earnings, CoreWeave owed more than $35 billion, partly because it pioneered using GPUs as collateral for loans. The Verge says the company lost more than a billion dollars in the first half of the year.

The article's author is not convinced this means the AI bubble is bursting. CoreWeave reported $103.7 billion in remaining performance obligations from customers, about 40 percent of it due in 2028, and those contracts can be cancelled only in limited circumstances. Microsoft, OpenAI and probably Nvidia, though CoreWeave does not name its third-largest customer, generated almost three-quarters of second-quarter revenue. The author considers OpenAI the shakiest of the three.

The worry has spread. Oracle's shares have fallen almost 10 percent over the same period, and there has been a sell-off in Oracle bonds. The Verge says the anxiety applies to neoclouds generally, though some investors are buying the dip.

A federal magistrate judge in San Francisco ruled Monday that Abdulrahman Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a covert recording device in a company conference room, must stay in custody while awaiting trial. Judge Alex Tse cited concerns about the defendant's ties to Saudi Arabia, according to Wired.

Prosecutors argued Alfozan is a flight risk because the Saudi government has offered unconditional support, including a consulate offer to work with a bail bonds firm. Tse called a government-backed bond "a blank check" and said he preferred family members putting up assets. Ars Technica reports prosecutors also said the FBI found a folder labeled "Saudi Gov Docs" on his iPhone, and that he has at least two Saudi bank accounts.

Prosecutors allege he messaged a member of the Saudi royal family on WhatsApp who was recruiting him for an AI initiative. They also say the Saudi government bought tickets for his wife and infant son to leave the country. His attorneys said the wife needed to renew a student visa and that her flight was booked by her sister's husband in his personal capacity. Attorney William Pernik called the flight risk worries baseless and said there was no evidence of spying for Saudi Arabia. Authorities have not offered a motive.

OpenAI found the device in late September and fired him this month. Alfozan faces up to five years on one count of using a device to intercept communications, and more charges are possible. Authorities say the device's data was encrypted, so it is unclear what was recorded. Pernik said he would keep fighting the ruling. The next court date is November 6. Saudi Arabia has not responded to requests for comment.

A Russian military satellite, Cosmos 2612, spent several days maneuvering very close to a US-operated commercial radar imaging satellite, ICEYE-X36, according to the orbital tracking firm LeoLabs. The company said the Russian craft closed from hundreds of kilometers away, moved around the satellite, stayed nearby and then began moving away.

Ars Technica reports that Cosmos 2612 was holding station 2 to 3 kilometers from the ICEYE craft by Friday and came within 500 meters over the weekend, likely closer, according to LeoLabs' Adam Marsh. Cosmos 2612 launched in April. LeoLabs called the behavior consistent with sophisticated rendezvous and proximity operations, not a routine flyby. Marsh and other analysts said it is the first such approach without the owner's consent in low-Earth orbit.

ICEYE is a Finnish company, and its US subsidiary owns ICEYE-X36. The satellite is widely believed to provide imagery to Ukraine, though Breaking Defense notes that has not been publicly confirmed. Ars Technica reports a Russian official said in 2022 that civilian satellites supporting Ukraine's military are a "legitimate target." An ICEYE US spokesperson said the company is tracking the situation and that its constellation is designed for continuity and resilience.

Analysts differed in emphasis. Clayton Swope of CSIS said policymakers should assume Cosmos 2612 could act against the satellite. Retired Lt. Gen. John Shaw called it a provocation and a message. Victoria Samson of Secure World Foundation wondered why the US government has been silent. No physical damage had been reported by Sunday, and Cosmos 2612 was moving away on Monday.

Finland is seeking to acquire one million anti-personnel mines in a plan costing 100 million euros, about $112 million, according to Al Jazeera. The plan follows Finland's withdrawal from the Ottawa Convention, the UN-backed treaty rejecting such munitions.

Colonel Riku Mikkonen of the Army Command told Finnish news agency STT that officials are gathering information from suppliers. Helsinki would like domestic manufacturers to build the mines, with contracts signed by the end of 2027 and production running by 2028. About half a dozen Finnish firms qualify, he said, though buying from abroad is not ruled out at this stage.

Finland joined the treaty in 2012. It announced its withdrawal in April 2025, citing a worsening security climate, and stopped being bound by the treaty in January. Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland also quit the agreement, citing the potential threat from Moscow. Al Jazeera notes that Russia is increasingly accused of hybrid warfare against supporters of Ukraine and possibly of planning military provocations.

Prime Minister Petteri Orpo has called Russia a long-term threat. Finland shares a border of roughly 1,340 kilometers with Russia and has strengthened its defenses since Moscow's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. It has also reported that migrants have been pushed across the border from the east.

Separately, Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen urged the EU on Monday to stop issuing tourist visas to Russians until the war ends. She noted that Schengen countries granted nearly half a million such visas in 2025, and that Finland banned them in 2022.

A wave of drone attacks across Sudan has killed more than 160 people in recent days, according to medics and rights groups cited by Al Jazeera. Emergency Lawyers, a group that monitors violence against civilians, said drone attacks on Khartoum killed three children on Monday. More than 160 deaths were reported in western regions since Friday.

The deadliest attack hit a transport hub near a market in Al-Dibab, in RSF-controlled West Kordofan state, on Sunday evening. Residents and medical workers said a drone killed 80 people, and a medical source told AFP that 30 of 47 wounded people later died. The RSF's self-declared administration, Tasis, and Emergency Lawyers accused the army of carrying out the attack.

Other incidents were attributed to both sides. Emergency Lawyers said an RSF drone attack on Friday hit displaced people in Blue Nile province, killing 41. A military source said air defenses intercepted RSF drones aimed at two dams in Gadaref state, and the RSF did not immediately comment. A drone strike on Nyala, an RSF stronghold, killed 17, including seven RSF officers, according to medical and RSF sources.

The UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said the organization is alarmed by the strikes, which are killing civilians and disrupting central services. The war between the army and the RSF began in April 2023. ACLED says it has killed at least 59,000 people, and aid groups say the true toll is likely higher. The UN says about 13 million people have been displaced.
On Friday, the United States urged the UN Security Council to push for a humanitarian truce and expand an arms embargo. China and Russia opposed widening the embargo.

Florida has issued an arrest warrant for 95-year-old former Cuban leader Raul Castro, Al Jazeera reports. State Attorney General James Uthmeier said Monday that the warrant rests on state charges of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder over Castro's alleged role in ordering the shootdown of two unarmed aircraft in 1996.

The planes were affiliated with Brothers to the Rescue, a Florida-based group that helps Cubans fleeing the country. Four people were killed on February 24, 1996. US authorities say the planes were over international waters and received no warning. Cuban officials have argued that earlier Brothers to the Rescue flights breached Cuban airspace despite warnings. Castro was defense minister at the time and later served as president from 2008 to 2018. Al Jazeera reports Cuba's response to the new warrant was not included in its article.

The state action follows a federal indictment unveiled in May that charges Castro with conspiracy to kill US nationals, destroying aircraft and four counts of murder. US Attorney Jason Reding Quinones said the administration backs "parallel federal and state prosecutions" and that the federal case laid the groundwork for Florida's.

Al Jazeera places the move in the context of the Trump administration's signaled desire for regime change in Cuba. It reports the administration imposed a de facto energy blockade in January by threatening tariffs on countries that supply Cuba with oil, and has added sanctions on state-run industries. Experts say this has worsened conditions on the island. The article also notes Trump has previously used indictments to justify military operations against leaders such as Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro.

A spacecraft has launched from Japan toward Mars's moon Phobos, where it will try to collect dust and bring it back to Earth, the BBC reports. If it succeeds, it will be the first time a sample from Mars or its moons has been returned for laboratory analysis. The Mars Moons Exploration mission, led by the Japanese space agency, is due to reach Phobos in August 2027.

The spacecraft will study the smaller moon Deimos on its way in, then focus on Phobos. It plans to set down a small rover to scout a landing site. Sara Russell of the Natural History Museum, a deputy for sample analysis, said landing a rover on such a small moon is hard because Phobos has little gravity of its own while sitting next to a planet with much stronger gravity. Once on the surface, the craft will use a robotic arm and two samplers to collect about 10 grams. A capsule is due to land in the Woomera desert of South Australia in 2031.

Scientists hope the material will settle how Mars's moons formed. One idea is that a space rock hit Mars early in its history and created them from debris. The other is that they are asteroids captured by Mars's gravity. Russell said the chemistry and minerals would point clearly to one explanation. The sample might also contain grains of Mars knocked onto Phobos by impacts.

The BBC notes the NASA and ESA Mars Sample Return mission has been effectively cancelled after Congress halted its funding. China plans its own Mars sampling mission, set to launch in 2028 and return material in 2031.

Amazon Web Services released a tool on Monday called TorchNeuron, which TechCrunch reports lets AI startups move their apps onto Amazon's Trainium chip. It works with PyTorch, the free, open source toolkit developers use to build, train and run AI models. According to Amazon, apps written with PyTorch can run on Trainium by changing one line of configuration, with no code rewrite.

The tool targets Nvidia's software advantage. Amazon says about 85 percent of AI apps are written with PyTorch, and Nvidia has spent years making its CUDA software support PyTorch, which TechCrunch says has embedded Nvidia hardware in the toolkit by default. Amazon is not the first to try. PyTorch users can already port apps to AMD GPUs or Apple chips with a simple configuration change.

Colin Brace, an AWS Annapurna Labs executive, told TechCrunch that building on AWS means not betting on a single-purpose compute provider. Amazon contrasts itself with neoclouds such as CoreWeave, Nebius and Firmus, many of which are tied to Nvidia. AWS says Trainium handles both training and inference and integrates tightly with its cloud, which it argues saves money even if it is not the cheapest per token. Brace cited the voice AI company Deepgram, which he said now processes 70 percent more audio per dollar.

Amazon also says it is contributing code to the main PyTorch project to remove ties to specific chips and make the framework more hardware-agnostic. TechCrunch notes that this benefits companies competing with Nvidia, and that it remains to be seen whether developers end up with more choice and lower costs, as Amazon promises, or simply more configuration headaches.

Microsoft on Monday introduced new security features meant to protect companies from the risks of AI agents, TechCrunch reports. The main addition is Guardian Agents, which monitors the AI agents a company uses. It is part of Project Perception, introduced in June with red, blue and green teams that attack, detect and fix vulnerabilities. TechCrunch says that design assumed AI hackers would come from outside the company.

CEO Satya Nadella has recently warned that the threat may be the agents enterprises deploy, much like a rogue employee. In a blog post earlier this month, he said companies should not rely on model providers' assurances and should use separate systems, not controlled by the AI labs, to watch and control agents. "We need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it," he wrote. Hayete Gallot, Microsoft's security business chief, wrote that frontier models "cannot be trusted," not because they are malicious or easily hacked but because they are unpredictable and trained to achieve tasks, not follow organizational norms.

Microsoft also added a feature to Defender that can detect up to 60 types of agents employees bring to work, including Claude Code, Codex and OpenClaw. New controls limit agents' access to data and systems, adjust permissions by task and require human approval when an agent appears to be making risky decisions.

TechCrunch calls the approach both surprising and self-serving. Microsoft has invested in OpenAI and Anthropic, yet wants customers to buy agent security from it instead of from those labs. The outlet adds that the idea is spreading: Microsoft joined Nvidia's Open Agent Safety Platform, backed by more than 100 other tech companies, which isolates agents and can stop their behavior through hardware.

OpenCode, an open source AI coding agent that developers use as an alternative to Claude Code and Cursor, said Saturday that attackers broke into an older system overnight. According to TechCrunch, the breach affected 1.4% of users of OpenCode Console, its online platform, where some users store the API keys they use to access AI services.

The company wrote on X that it was a "large-scale distillation attack" and that it had emailed all affected users. It did not say how the attack worked. Some skeptics called that framing an overstretch, arguing the incident was a straightforward breach and that its use for distillation remains unproven.

Developers posted spending alerts and unauthorized charges on Reddit and X. Some reported charges in the hundreds of dollars, and a few said totals topped $1,000. Anthropic and Google blocked the keys they believed were exposed, while OpenAI said it worked with OpenCode to restore access and refund its API customers. OpenCode said refunds are underway. Co-founder Dax Raad said the open source app and command-line tool were not affected.

Raad said attackers had tried to break in nonstop for 48 hours. AI models the team used for analysis began refusing to work when the malicious code tripped safety filters. OpenCode later got access to OpenAI's Daybreak Blue program, which gives vetted users models less likely to refuse defensive security work. David Sacks, co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, wrote on X that the guardrails backfired.

OpenCode has not detailed how attackers got into the older system, how keys were stored or the full extent of misuse. It has told affected users to revoke and replace their keys with each provider, and it said the incident remains ongoing.

Town, a two-year-old San Francisco startup building AI assistants, announced a $108 million Series B round on Monday, giving it a unicorn valuation, according to TechCrunch. Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures co-led the round, with Andreessen Horowitz, Serena Ventures and First Round Capital also participating. The company launched publicly four months ago and said it reached millions of dollars in annual recurring revenue within weeks. It has raised at least $160 million, including a $55 million Series A announced in June.

Town was founded by former Plaid CTO Jean-Denis Greze and targets businesses. Each employee gets an AI assistant called a Townie that connects to tools such as email and calendars. Townies can talk to each other and share approved information, and they can now also work with customers and people outside the company. Alongside the funding, Town announced a shared workflow that automatically updates every Townie with new business information.

Separately, TechCrunch reported that Tolan, an AI companion app meant to help people manage daily life, relationships and emotions, raised $30 million from investors including Union Square Ventures, Khosla Ventures and Homebrew. Tolan did not disclose its new valuation; PitchBook estimates it at more than $268 million, with medium confidence. The company told Upstarts Media its annual recurring revenue is in the double-digit millions, and it claims more than 250,000 active users.

TechCrunch noted risks for Tolan, including competition from AI agents that complete tasks, such as Meta's Muse, and multiple lawsuits against general-purpose chatbot makers alleging chatbot interactions contributed to users' suicides.

The United States is building more fossil fuel infrastructure than it has in a decade while renewable energy growth slows, according to a report published last week by the nonprofit Environmental Defense Fund and the research firm Atlas Public Policy. The report analyzes data from the US Energy Information Administration, and The Verge summarized its findings.

Plans for new fossil fuel infrastructure rose from 5 percent of all new capacity in 2024 to 30 percent by the second quarter of 2026. If the trend continues, fossil fuels could make up 70 percent of the development pipeline by the end of the decade. Planned fossil capacity would reach 68 gigawatts by 2030, a 45 percent jump from plans six months ago. The report says renewable projects are being canceled faster than fossil ones, at 4.9 percent compared with 2.9 percent.

Electricity demand is climbing faster than it has in more than a decade as data centers, factories and electric vehicles connect to the grid. The Verge says the Trump administration has sought to hobble wind and solar through stop work orders, blocked permits and removed tax incentives, while favoring fossil fuels for data centers. The article notes a rush of new solar and wind farms continues, many from the last wave of projects that benefited from Biden-era incentives.

On cost, the report finds new utility-scale solar and wind average $68 to $69 per megawatt-hour, versus $90 for new combined-cycle gas plants. Its authors warn that if all gas projects in the pipeline are built, they could lock in more pollution and higher electricity prices for decades. The Verge notes many plans could still fall through, particularly if forecasts for AI data center demand prove overblown. The administration's response was not included in the page text.

President Trump signed an executive order on Monday creating a women's health division within the National Institutes of Health and a White House task force on the subject. First lady Melania Trump, who announced the initiative, said, "Beginning today, we will change the reality of women's health." The order requires the NIH division to be set up within 90 days.

According to STAT, the division is meant to streamline research into understudied diseases in women, advance diagnostics and improve treatment. An NIH spokesperson said it would also strengthen the inclusion of women and girls in clinical trials. It does not replace the NIH Office of Research on Women's Health, and Al Jazeera, citing the White House, reported it will have a broader mandate beyond research.

The task force will be led by White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. also named as a co-chair by Al Jazeera. Members include Pete Hegseth, acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas and CDC Director Erica Schwartz. The Department of Health and Human Services will pay the task force's administrative costs, but the order includes no specific funding targets or dollar amounts.

Critics questioned its effectiveness. Al Jazeera cited layoffs of thousands of NIH employees, a deadline to cut spending by 35 percent, and the 2025 move to end regional contracts for the Women's Health Initiative. STAT reported that scientists said women's health work was put at risk early in the administration by scrutiny of grants. The White House's response to those criticisms was not in the page text. Details of the new NIH division have not been disclosed.

Senate Republicans forced a vote on the Ratepayer Protection Act, a measure aimed at curbing utility costs tied to building data centers. According to Fox News chief congressional correspondent reporting in a Reporter's Notebook, Democrats blocked it, along with a separate bill to restrict stock trades by lawmakers that included a voter ID requirement.

Republicans argued the bill responds to voter concern. Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said people should be guaranteed that electricity bills will not rise "by a cent" because of a data center. Democrats said the bill has no force. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., called it "a sham," and Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said everything in it can already be done by a state regulator or developer. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., called it "a toothless messaging bill."

Both sides acknowledged the politics. Democrats said Republicans called the vote to help Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who faces former Sen. Sherrod Brown in a closely watched race. Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., said "I think it will help him." Husted said, "We gave everybody a chance to do something about affordability and the Democrats blocked it. So we'll go campaign on it."

The article notes Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., said on September 23 that he supported the bill, then voted no. He said Democrats were not allowed an amendment and that the bill "has no teeth." Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., called the issue a "no brainer." The article says an August internal GOP memo showed concern about how data centers could affect Husted.

Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar and Republican state House Speaker Lisa Demuth met in their first debate in Minnesota's governor race, and the state's welfare assistance fraud scandal dominated the first half, according to Fox News. The schemes involved pandemic-era social services and siphoned hundreds of millions of dollars, and potentially billions, from federal and state programs. The scandal led Gov. Tim Walz, a Democrat, to abandon his re-election bid.

Demuth said, "We have allowed a culture of waste and fraud to go on far too long." She asked Klobuchar why she did not do more, and why she missed Senate hearings on fraud. Klobuchar said she would have caught the fraud and that when it went public she called the Justice Department and asked for more resources, which she said led to more federal prosecutors being assigned. She said she had attended a dozen hearings where she asked about fraud, and that the hearing Demuth cited was of a subcommittee she was not on. Demuth also pledged to fire all of the state's commissioners to start fresh.

The candidates also sparred over health care. Demuth blamed the Affordable Care Act for rising costs and said it had not delivered on promises of affordability. Klobuchar's response on that point was not in the page text. Both said they would not raise taxes.

Fox News reported that polls show Klobuchar leading by an upper single-digit margin, and its Power Rankings rate the race Likely Democrat. Demuth is seeking to be the first Republican in twenty years to win a Minnesota governor's race.

A Kansas man, Jaden John Read, has been charged with threatening to kill President Trump, according to the Washington Examiner. The federal criminal complaint, filed Oct. 17, accuses him of knowingly and willfully threatening to take the president's life or inflict bodily harm. The charge carries a maximum sentence of five years in prison. The complaint contains allegations, and the page text does not include a response from Read.

According to an affidavit signed by a Secret Service officer, Read allegedly posted comments on Facebook on Oct. 15 in response to news articles about Trump's Monday visit to Wichita. One allegedly said, "Lets shoot Trump honestly. Where's our shooter?" Another allegedly claimed he had obtained rifle rounds. A third, allegedly posted in response to a KWCH 12 News article, said he had "already mapped out roofs around" where the speech would be.

The complaint says Wichita Police Deputy Chief Dan East contacted the Secret Service on Oct. 15 after a Crime Stoppers tip, and provided screenshots of the comments. Secret Service investigators then located the additional comment about the speech and rooftops. Beyond prison time, the complaint lists up to three years of supervised release, a fine of up to $250,000 and a $100 special assessment.

Trump was scheduled to hold a Monday evening rally in Wichita to campaign for Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., who faces Democrat Adam Hamilton. The Examiner cited a RealClearPolitics average showing Marshall ahead 46% to 45.7%. No Democrat has won a Kansas Senate seat since 1932.

The Mississippi attorney general's office announced Monday that the police shooting of one-year-old Kohen Wiley "was justified," according to The Guardian. The announcement came four months after the child was killed in Senatobia, Mississippi, while sitting in his mother's lap.

On June 14, officers responded to a shoplifting call alleging that the baby's mother, Vellesiya Wiley, and a friend, Latoya Ferrell, had taken a pack of diapers. Neither woman has been charged, and officials have not released evidence of shoplifting. Police reports say the women and child entered a vehicle and began leaving the parking lot when officers arrived and drew weapons. Wiley lifted the baby to show a child was in the car. Sgt Hunter Foster fired into the vehicle, killing Kohen and wounding Ferrell.

The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation alleged the driver "drove in the direction of the officers, almost striking one." Attorney Ben Crump, who represents the family, released an independent autopsy indicating Kohen was shot from the side of the car, not the front, which he said contradicted officers' statements. It is not clear if or when footage will be released. Crump has said the family has not been allowed to see it.

The Guardian noted prior controversies in Senatobia's police department. The town fired its police chief in September after he reportedly used racial slurs, and in 2023 an officer arrested a 10-year-old Black boy for urinating in public. Angelica Maze has replaced the chief, Harold Vanderford. The page text does not include a response from the family to the ruling.

Paul Mackenzie, leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult, has been found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, according to the BBC. Justice Diana Mochache delivered an eight-hour judgment in Mombasa. Twenty-eight other cult leaders were also convicted of murder. They had pleaded not guilty and repeatedly insisted that nobody was forced to die.

The court heard that Mackenzie ordered members to starve their children so they could "meet Jesus." His doctrine held that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil." The judge said followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece" and that burials in the forest were called "weddings." One co-accused said Mackenzie told followers that anyone who resisted fasting must be forced to heaven "through kicks and blows." His former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, took a plea deal and testified for the prosecution.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after more than 400 bodies were found in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. Gravediggers told the BBC that every grave they found held at least three bodies. Many remain unidentified. Stephen Mwiti said he lost all six of his children to the cult and that his former wife was among those convicted. He said he was happy that all had been convicted.

Mackenzie founded Good News International Ministries in 2003 and moved to the forest after the main church shut in 2019. He is due to be sentenced on 6 November. He and other leaders also face other cases, including terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children.

Israeli police said they detained 10 people after a weekend of violence in the West Bank, according to The Guardian. Police released footage of the raid on Monday and said the detentions were connected with attacks on foreigners and the construction of an illegal outpost. A court later extended the detention of six men tied to the attacks on foreigners to between three and four days.

On Friday, US photojournalist Heidi Levine was beaten by masked Israeli men while covering an olive harvest near Ramallah. She said her injuries included four broken vertebrae and a finger that needed surgery, and she called it an "attempted lynching." The next day, men armed with sticks and iron bars attacked European diplomats and Palestinians harvesting olives near Taybeh, assaulting a French mayor and badly injuring a young Palestinian man, the Guardian reported.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu referred to an "alleged attack" on Levine and "unproven allegations" about the diplomats. The Guardian said this ignored video and witness evidence, and described the statements as seen as an appeal to far-right voters before an election. The attacks drew criticism from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, US Ambassador Mike Huckabee and European countries. Netanyahu's office was not quoted responding to the arrests.

Levine said Palestinians face similar attacks with little response. Yesh Din documented 561 incidents of settler and soldier violence against Palestinians since September 27, and said 94% of investigations into settler violence are closed without indictments. Haaretz reported that defense officials say commanders are reluctant to confront settler leaders.

A newly released report says a wildlife overpass above a busy stretch of Interstate 25 in Colorado has cut wildlife-vehicle collisions by 91% in the 10 months since it was completed, according to The Guardian. Officials have tracked elk, bears, pronghorn and northern leopard frogs crossing it.

The Colorado Department of Transportation said the corridor averaged one wildlife-vehicle crash a day before the overpass was built. The structure sits between Denver and Colorado Springs, spans six lanes of traffic and connects 39,000 acres of habitat on both sides of the interstate. It is covered in grass, measures 200 feet wide and 209 feet long, and has gradually sloped entrances to ease crossings for animals.

State officials say underpasses and tunnels often do not work for large animals such as elk, because they restrict movement and do not accommodate antlers. Chuck Attardo, the department's environmental manager, told CBS News that elk and pronghorn prefer big open structures where they can see for miles. He said pronghorn had looked for a place to cross I-25 for decades, and that video now shows them using the overpass and reaching the west side for the first time in decades. Officials have also recorded mule deer, coyotes, rabbits, frogs and the threatened Preble's meadow jumping mouse.

The project received $22 million in federal funding and $8 million from the state, but officials say it was finished for $15 million. Nearly 20 wildlife crossings are under way in the US, and Colorado's is currently the biggest. Research has shown such overpasses can nearly eliminate these collisions and often pay for themselves by preventing costly crashes. The transportation department says it hopes to build other wildlife crossings across the state.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced on Monday that the state will receive a $6 million settlement payment in 23andMe's bankruptcy. The payment resolves California's legal claims over a 2023 data breach that exposed genetic and other personal information of 6.9 million customers, according to The Guardian. The attorney general's office said the breach affected more than 855,000 Californians.

California had unsuccessfully tried to block the $305 million sale of 23andMe assets to TTAM Research Institute, a nonprofit controlled by 23andMe co-founder Anne Wojcicki. The state argued the sale violated California's Genetic Information Privacy Act and that consumers had not given express consent. Customers kept the option to delete their data during the sale process, but California said the court should have barred any data transfer unless customers first gave express consent.

A US bankruptcy judge ruled against California's objections and later ruled the state could not sue to recover money from the bankrupt company's successor. California also lost an appeal in federal district court. According to court documents filed Monday, it agreed to drop further appeals as part of the settlement.

Bonta, a Democrat, said in a statement that he was proud to fight for Californians' privacy rights and reminded them that 23andMe customers can delete their genetic data no matter who owns it. 23andMe, which filed for bankruptcy in March 2025 after a decline in demand and legal fallout from the breach, had separately agreed to pay $46.75 million to breach victims as part of the bankruptcy.
